claim: Phage pressure accelerated capsule inactivation.

claim: BJ1 clones quickly become lysogens with high induction rates which leads to their removal from the population by the end of the experimental evolution.

claim: High BJ1 frequencies in MMC populations are potentially linked to the emergence of diverse resistance mechanisms imposing lower fitness costs.
source: High BJ1 frequencies in these populations are potentially linked to the emergence of diverse resistance mechanisms imposing lower fitness costs (Figure 4).
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: Non-capsulated clones are fitter at the early stages of the coevolution, but capsulated non-lysogenized BJ1-resistant clones may outcompete other resistant BJ1 at longer evolutionary time scales.
source: Indeed, non-capsulated clones are fitter at the early stages of the coevolution, but capsulated non-lysogenized BJ1-resistant clones may outcompete other resistant BJ1 at longer evolutionary time scales.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Lysogenization is not a stable mechanism of defense in this system.
source: We now show that lysogenization is not a stable mechanism of defense in this system (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Lysogenization results in high rates of spontaneous phage induction that lead to cell death.
source: This is because it results in high rates of spontaneous phage induction that lead to cell death.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental observations

claim: High induction rates of phage lambda decreased the fitness of lysogens in E. coli in a murine model.
source: Similar observations were made with E. coli in a murine model in which high induction rates of phage lambda decreased the fitness of lysogens (De Paepe et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to De Paepe et al., 2016

claim: After lysogenization, phage induction was very high, but this was followed by progressive domestication.
source: Frazão et al., 2022 also observed that after lysogenization, phage induction was very high, however, this was followed by progressive domestication, suggesting that the cost of some resistant mechanisms can be overcome.
evidence: Supported by citation to Frazão et al., 2022

claim: Lysogenic conversion was less frequent (~50% less) when a non-lysogenic P. aeruginosa was competed against a polylysogenic strain, compared to conditions when it was exposed to a single-lysogenized strain.
source: For instance, lysogenic conversion was less frequent (~50% less) when a non-lysogenic P. aeruginosa was competed against a polylysogenic strain, compared to conditions when it was exposed to a single-lysogenized strain (Burns et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burns et al., 2015

claim: Lysogeny is disfavoured as a mechanism of phage resistance when the rates of spontaneous induction are high, when bacteria are targeted by multiple different phages, or when other less costly alternative resistant mechanisms may emerge.
source: Overall, lysogeny is disfavoured as a mechanism of phage resistance when the rates of spontaneous induction are high, when bacteria are targeted by multiple different phages, or when other less costly alternative resistant mechanisms may emerge.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations and literature

claim: The dominant type of resistance mechanisms changes across evolutionary time scales.
source: A major finding of our work is that the dominant type of the resistance mechanisms changes across evolutionary time scales.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations

claim: At first, resistance emerged quickly to the loss of capsule production because functional inactivation can be achieved in many ways.
source: At first, resistance emerged quickly to the loss of capsule production because functional inactivation can be achieved in many ways (Chiarelli et al., 2020; Haudiquet et al., 2021; Nucci et al., 2022; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 2 and citations to Chiarelli et al., 2020; Haudiquet et al., 2021; Nucci et al., 2022

claim: At later stages, resistance may emerge by changes in the composition or expression of the capsule, which can outcompete both lysogens and non-capsulated clones.
source: At later stages, resistance may emerge by changes in the composition or expression of the capsule, which can outcompete both lysogens and non-capsulated clones.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Some phage-resistant clones reverted to susceptibility after two passages in the absence of phage pressure.
source: Surprisingly, our study revealed that some phage-resistant clones reverted to susceptibility after two passages in the absence of phage pressure.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: The sequence of clones that reverted to susceptibility failed to reveal any mutations that could explain the phenotypic change.
source: Yet, the sequence of these clones failed to reveal any mutations that could explain the phenotypic change.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data analysis

claim: Almost half of 57 different clones of K. pneumoniae resistant to a virulent phage lacked identifiable mutations.
source: For instance, Hesse and colleagues sequenced 57 different clones of K. pneumoniae resistant to a virulent phage and found that almost half of them lacked identifiable mutations (Hesse et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hesse et al., 2020

claim: The nucleotide sequence of the gene wcaJ of the K2 capsule has short simple sequence repeats (SSR) whose changes are difficult to detect with current genome assemblers and variant calling software.
source: Our clones could be transiently resistant because the nucleotide sequence of the gene wcaJ of the K2 capsule has short simple sequence repeats (SSR) whose changes are difficult to detect with the current genome assemblers and variant calling software.
evidence: Speculation about potential mechanism

claim: SSR are often mutational hotspots allowing rapid evolution of traits by changes that are easily reversible.
source: SSR are often mutational hotspots allowing rapid evolution of traits by changes that are easily reversible (Moxon et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moxon et al., 1994

claim: Capsule inactivation in ST14 is associated with an insertion of a thymine among a repeat of thymine residues.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, we found that capsule inactivation in ST14 is associated with an insertion of a thymine among a repeat of thymine residues (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data in Supplementary file 2

claim: Epigenetic-based resistance based on DNA modifications, such as methylation, can regulate the length of the O-antigen in Salmonella enterica and result in transient phage resistance.
source: One is the epigenetic-based resistance based on DNA modifications, such as methylation. This was previously shown to regulate the length of the O-antigen length by phase variation in Salmonella enterica, and resulted in transient phage resistance (Cota et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cota et al., 2015

claim: Transient cell wall shedding in filamentous actinobacteria, B. subtilis and E. coli can lead to transient phage resistance.
source: Additionally, transient cell wall shedding in filamentous actinobacteria, B. subtilis and E. coli (Ongenae et al., 2022) and conversion to cell wall-deficient L-forms in Listeria monocytogenes (Wohlfarth et al., 2023) can lead to transient phage resistance.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ongenae et al., 2022 and Wohlfarth et al., 2023

claim: Conversion to cell wall-deficient L-forms in Listeria monocytogenes can lead to transient phage resistance.
source: Additionally, transient cell wall shedding in filamentous actinobacteria, B. subtilis and E. coli (Ongenae et al., 2022) and conversion to cell wall-deficient L-forms in Listeria monocytogenes (Wohlfarth et al., 2023) can lead to transient phage resistance.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wohlfarth et al., 2023

claim: Non-genetic protective changes are comparable to inducible immune responses (CRISPR-Cas) that incur lower fitness costs relative to other constitutive changes such as permanent loss of receptors.
source: Such non-genetic protective changes are comparable to inducible immune responses (CRISPR-Cas) that incur in lower fitness costs relative to other constitutive changes such as permanent loss of receptors (Westra et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Westra et al., 2015

claim: At a longer evolutionary time scale, non-genetic modifications or inducible resistance can emerge.
source: Here, we show that at a longer evolutionary time scale, non-genetic modifications or inducible resistance can emerge.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations

claim: Non-genetic mechanisms do not result in added cost and bacteria can revert to susceptibility once phage pressure is relieved.
source: Contrary to a constitutive inactivation of the capsule, non-genetic mechanisms do not result in added cost and the bacteria can revert to susceptibility once phage pressure is relieved.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental observations

claim: The efficiency and fitness costs of phage-resistance mechanisms are context-dependent, as they can impose trade-offs in different environmental conditions.
source: Both the efficiency and fitness costs of phage-resistance mechanisms are context-dependent, as they can impose trade-offs in different environmental conditions (Meaden et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meaden et al., 2015

claim: Some mutants were only resistant to phages in liquid media but remained fully sensitive to the same phages when growing on agar.
source: We found that some mutants were only resistant to phages in liquid media, i.e., in the environment where they evolved, but remained fully sensitive to the same phages when growing on agar.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: Phage-resistant Pseudomonas syringae evolved in vitro did not display a fitness advantage compared to phage-sensitive cells when grown on a plant surface in the presence of phage.
source: This recapitulates phage-resistant Pseudomonas syringae evolved in vitro that did not display a fitness advantage compared to phage-sensitive cells when grown on a plant surface in the presence of phage (Hernandez and Koskella, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hernandez and Koskella, 2019

claim: Phage-sensitive bacteria are able to survive phage attacks in structured environments (agar, gut, or plant surface) due to the existence of refuges where sensitive cells may evade the phage.
source: These results are unexpected given previous studies showing that phage-sensitive bacteria are able to survive phage attacks in structured environments (agar, gut, or plant surface) due to the existence of refuges where sensitive cells may evade the phage (Lourenço et al., 2020; Eriksen et al., 2018; Schrag and Mittler, 1996; Simmons et al., 2020; Testa et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lourenço et al., 2020; Eriksen et al., 2018; Schrag and Mittler, 1996; Simmons et al., 2020; Testa et al., 2019

claim: Survival in refuges is often contingent on the presence of other phage-resistant clones, or enhanced phenotypic resistance in structured environments due to reduced receptor expression.
source: However, survival in refuges is often contingent on the presence of other phage-resistant clones, or enhanced phenotypic resistance in structured environments due to reduced receptor expression (Attrill et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Attrill et al., 2021

claim: In well-shaken liquid, phage-bacterium interactions are unstable, compared to interactions on agar.
source: A plausible explanation could be that in well-shaken liquid, phage-bacterium interactions are unstable, compared to interactions on agar (Brockhurst et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brockhurst et al., 2006

claim: Less capsulated mutants could attain a higher level of resistance in liquid than in solid.
source: If this is true, then less capsulated mutants could attain a higher level of resistance in liquid than in solid.
evidence: Speculation based on previous observation

claim: The ΔrcsB mutant that produces fewer capsule remains equally sensitive to phage in both liquid and agar.
source: Yet, resistance is not necessarily linked to a mere reduction in the production of the capsule because the ∆rcsB mutant that produces fewer capsule remains equally sensitive to phage in both liquid and agar (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5
